questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: One method for two identical requirements
questions.learningObjective: supply the single method that satisfies two interfaces declaring the same signature

options.text: public String name() { return "thing"; }  one method of that signature serves both interfaces.
public String count() { return "thing"; }  any public method satisfies a declared interface method.
options.misconception: believes a method of any name implements an interface requirement

options.text: public int name() { return 1; }  the return type does not have to agree with the declaration.
options.misconception: believes the return type may differ when implementing an interface

options.text: public String name();  an abstract declaration is enough inside a concrete class.
options.misconception: believes restating the method without a body implements it

questions.explanation: The rule is that an interface requirement is met by a public instance method with exactly that name, parameter list and return type, so one String name() covers both Named and Countable because their declarations are identical. Naming the method count() is tempting because the interface is called Countable, but the compiler matches on the declared signature rather than on anything the interface is named, and a method of the right name with the wrong return type does not count either, since String and int are unrelated types and no conversion bridges them.
questions.hint: The two interfaces declare the same signature, so one implementation can serve both.

The compiler rejects it, because only a method written in the class body can implement an interface.
options.misconception: believes an inherited method can never implement an interface method

options.text: "generic" only if Dog is declared abstract, otherwise the call through the interface fails.
options.misconception: believes the class must be abstract to inherit an implementation

options.text: null, because the interface declares speak and so it hides the superclass's version.
options.misconception: believes an interface declaration hides an inherited superclass method

questions.explanation: The rule is that a class is concrete when it has no abstract requirements left, and an inherited public method with the right signature satisfies the interface just as a declared one would, so the call dispatches to Animal.speak and prints generic. Believing an inherited method does not count is tempting because the code inside Dog is empty and looks unfinished, but the implements clause is a promise about the whole type, and the promise is kept by whatever public method the type already has. Had Animal's method been package-private, the compiler would have refused, because the interface demands public.
questions.hint: Ask which public method of the type, from anywhere in its ancestry, matches.

questions.topic: An ambiguous overload for a class that implements both
questions.learningObjective: predict that an argument satisfying two unrelated interfaces makes an overload call ambiguous

options.text: The compiler rejects the call with "reference to handle is ambiguous", since neither overload is more specific.
It compiles and prints "left", because the first applicable overload is the one that is chosen.
options.misconception: believes overload resolution takes the first applicable method

options.text: It compiles and prints "right", because the overload declared last is the one that is chosen.
options.misconception: believes overload resolution takes the most recently declared method

options.text: It compiles and prints "left" and then "right", since every matching overload is called.
options.misconception: believes an ambiguous call fans out to all matching overloads

questions.explanation: The rule is that overload resolution picks the most specific applicable method, and an argument that is both a Left and a Right matches both overloads equally well, so the compiler reports the call as ambiguous instead of guessing. Expecting the first declaration to win is tempting because the argument does fit handle(Left), but specificity is decided by the types rather than by their order in the file, and Left is not a supertype of Right, so a caller has to disambiguate explicitly, for example by casting or by calling a method that takes both parameters.
questions.hint: Neither parameter type is a supertype of the other, so neither overload is more specific.

questions.topic: Two constants with one simple name

options.misconception: believes the first interface in the list supplies the constant

options.text: It compiles and returns 2, because the interface listed last donates its constant.
options.misconception: believes the last interface in the list supplies the constant

options.text: It compiles and returns 3, because a class gets a constant of its own from two interfaces.

Expecting list order to decide is tempting because the compiler does prefer a class's own field over an inherited one, but that preference is about hiding rather than about a tie, and nothing here declares a field, so the two inherited constants stand in equal competition until the source names one of them.
questions.hint: Nothing in the class hides either constant, so the simple name has two sources.

options.misconception: believes a reference may call any method of the object it holds

questions.topic: Same name, different signatures
questions.learningObjective: count the methods a class needs when two interfaces declare the same name differently
questions.stem: One interface declares void log() and an unrelated interface declares void log(String detail). A single class implements both. How many methods must that class declare to satisfy the two requirements?

options.text: Two methods, log() and log(String), because a signature includes the parameter list as well as the name.
One method, log(), because the interface with the longer parameter list is the more specific one.
options.misconception: believes a longer parameter list makes one requirement subsume the other

options.text: One method, log(String), because an implementation may drop parameters a caller never passes.
options.misconception: believes an implementation may ignore part of a declared parameter list

options.text: Two methods, but only if the two interfaces are implemented by different classes.
options.misconception: believes the number of methods depends on which classes implement the interfaces

questions.hint: Compare the full signatures rather than just the method names.

questions.topic: A same-named method with the wrong return type

options.misconception: believes a matching name is enough to implement an interface method

questions.topic: A default method built on the abstract one
questions.learningObjective: trace a default method that calls the implementing class's version of the abstract method

options.text: "hi Ana": the default body calls who(), which dispatches to the class's implementation.
"hi null", because the default body runs without any state from the implementing class.
options.misconception: believes a default method sees nothing of the implementing class

options.text: "Ana", because implementing the abstract method replaces the default method's own body.
options.misconception: believes the class's method replaces the inherited default

options.text: It throws AbstractMethodError, because a default may not call an abstract method.
options.misconception: believes a default method cannot call an abstract method of its own interface

A default may freely call the interface's own abstract methods, since every implementer is obliged to supply them.
questions.hint: The default's body is inherited; the call inside it is dispatched normally.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Claims about a class that implements two interfaces
questions.learningObjective: judge which statements hold when one class implements two interfaces
questions.stem: A cheat sheet lists four claims about a class that implements two interfaces. Which claims are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A single public method can satisfy two interfaces that declare the same signature.
A public method inherited from a superclass can satisfy an interface requirement.
A method of the same name but a different return type satisfies the interface method.
options.misconception: believes a matching name is enough to implement a requirement

options.text: One method of either signature satisfies an overloaded pair of interface methods.
options.misconception: believes one method can cover two overloads at once

options.text: A constant inherited from two interfaces is used directly without qualifying it.
options.misconception: believes an ambiguous inherited constant may be used unqualified

The tempting shortcuts are all about relaxing the match: a shared name with a different return type is a different method, an overloaded pair needs two methods rather than one flexible one, and a constant that arrives from two unrelated interfaces has no single meaning until the source is named at the use site.
questions.hint: For each claim, ask whether one method with one signature could serve both roles.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: What a reference type lets you call
questions.learningObjective: apply that a reference's declared type governs which members may be called
questions.stem: A class Doc implements both Printable, which declares print(), and Saveable, which declares save(). A local variable is declared Printable p = new Doc();. Which calls on p are legal without a cast?

options.text: Only p.print(), because a Printable reference exposes the members Printable declares.
Both p.print() and p.save(), because the object behind p really is a Doc.
options.misconception: believes the runtime type of an object widens what a reference can call

options.text: Both p.print() and p.save(), because Doc implements both interfaces at compile time.
options.misconception: believes the class's interface list widens every reference to it

options.text: Neither, because a reference typed as an interface cannot reach any method at all.
options.misconception: believes an interface reference exposes nothing but the class's own methods

questions.explanation: The rule is that the compiler checks each call against the reference's declared type, so p.print() is accepted and p.save() is not, because Saveable is not part of Printable and the two interfaces are unrelated, so reaching save() needs a Saveable reference or a cast such as ((Saveable) p).save(). Expecting the object to widen what is callable is tempting because the value really is a Doc at run time, but the check is made on the static type precisely so that a caller is not surprised, and the class's own implementation of print is reached through the interface just as well.
questions.hint: The compiler only knows the type written in the declaration.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A diamond of default methods
questions.learningObjective: apply that the most specific inherited default wins in a hierarchy of interfaces

options.text: "beta": where one default extends another the more specific one wins, and Gamma adds nothing.
"alpha": the interface at the top of the chain is the one that supplies the method.
options.misconception: believes the topmost interface in a hierarchy wins a default conflict

options.text: The compiler rejects Leaf, because Alpha and Gamma both supply a who() to it.
options.misconception: believes an inherited default conflicts with the interface that redeclared it

options.text: "gamma", because the interface a class implements directly supplies the method itself.
options.misconception: believes the directly implemented interface contributes a default of its own

questions.explanation: The rule is that Beta's who() overrides the one it inherits from Alpha, so Beta is the most specific declaration in the chain and its body is the one Leaf inherits, while Gamma only extends Beta without restating anything. Reading the top of the chain as the winner is tempting because Alpha is where the method was written first, but override rules run from the most specific type downwards, and there is no conflict at all here, since a redeclaration in a subinterface replaces the inherited default rather than competing with it as an unrelated default would.
questions.hint: Work out which declaration overrides which along the extends chain.

questions.topic: The same chain with no redeclaration
questions.learningObjective: trace a default that is inherited unchanged by a subinterface

options.text: "alpha": Beta restates nothing, so the single default is inherited from Alpha unchanged.
"beta", because every subinterface supplies a default of its own for the same method.
options.misconception: believes a subinterface always donates a default implementation

options.text: It throws AbstractMethodError, because who() has no body inside the class that implements it.

options.text: The compiler rejects Leaf, because Leaf implements Beta without redeclaring who().

Expecting a subinterface to supply its own default is tempting because the subinterface is the more specific type and the most specific usually wins, but there is nothing more specific to win here since Beta never declared who(), and an inherited default is exactly as real as a declared one, which is why Leaf compiles with an empty body.
questions.hint: Inheritance carries the whole member along, body included.

questions.topic: Reaching a superclass from a default method

questions.topic: Naming both defaults from the class

options.text: return Alpha.super.who() + "/" + Beta.super.who();  a class may name either default that way.

questions.hint: The conflict is resolved in the class body, where each default can be named.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Claims about default methods
questions.learningObjective: judge which statements hold for inherited default methods
questions.stem: A reference lists four claims about default methods. Which claims are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A method written in the class takes precedence over any default it inherits.
Two unrelated interfaces with the same default name force the class to override it.
Where one default extends another, the more specific default is the one that runs.
A default may be called on the interface name, as in Alpha.who(), with no instance.

questions.topic: The narrowest useful parameter type
questions.learningObjective: choose a one-method interface as the parameter type of a read-only client
questions.stem: A report class reads one record by id and does nothing else. A store offers read, write, delete and count. Which parameter type belongs on the report's method?

options.text: A one-method interface declaring only read(int), so the report can be handed any reader and cannot write.
The four-method store interface, so every store passed in must offer all four operations.
options.misconception: believes the parameter type must list every method the implementation has

options.text: Object, so the report can accept any store at all without having to name it.
options.misconception: believes Object is the narrowest type that keeps the call legal

options.text: The concrete store class, so the report reads straight from that one implementation.
options.misconception: believes naming the concrete class is the way to keep a parameter narrow

Taking the fat store interface is tempting because it names the real object being passed, but it forces every future store to offer four operations for the sake of one, and using Object would compile only by giving up the ability to call read at all without a cast.
questions.hint: Name the operations the report actually calls, and nothing else.

questions.learningObjective: predict that a method missing from the reference's type cannot be called at all

options.text: The compiler rejects it: cannot find symbol, method setSize(int), because ReadonlyBox declares only size().
It compiles and prints 5, because the object behind the reference really is a Box.
options.misconception: believes the runtime class's methods are reachable through a narrow reference

options.text: It compiles and prints 3, because a read-only type drops writes instead of failing.
options.misconception: believes a write through a read-only type is silently ignored

options.text: It compiles and throws IllegalAccessException, because setSize is not part of the interface.
options.misconception: believes a method missing from an interface fails at run time instead

questions.explanation: The rule is that a method may only be called if the reference's declared type declares it, and ReadonlyBox declares just size(), so javac reports cannot find symbol for setSize(int) and the program never reaches its print. Believing the call works is tempting because the value really is a Box and Box does have that method, but the narrow type is exactly what prevents the write, and that prevention is the design working: the compiler has caught a mutation that the interface promised could not happen, rather than discovering it later at run time.
questions.hint: The declared type of b is the whole story the compiler has to go on.

questions.topic: A read through the read-only type
questions.learningObjective: trace a read that the narrow interface does allow

options.text: 3: size() is declared by the interface, so the call is legal and the implementation returns 3.
0: a read through an interface returns the interface's own default rather than the value.
options.misconception: believes a read through an interface yields a default instead of the value

options.text: It throws AbstractMethodError, because Box's size() is not inherited from the interface.
options.misconception: believes a method that supplies a requirement is not really the implementation

options.text: It throws NullPointerException, because the interface type cannot hold a class instance.
options.misconception: believes an interface reference may not refer to an implementing object

questions.explanation: The rule is that a call through an interface runs the implementing class's method, so b.size() is legal because ReadonlyBox declares it and it dispatches to Box.size, returning the 3 the constructor stored. Expecting a default is tempting because an interface declaration carries no state of its own, but the object behind the reference holds that state and the interface is only a way of naming the operations, so the value comes from the instance and the narrow type costs nothing for a read it allows.
questions.hint: The interface names the operation; the object supplies the value.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A lambda for a one-method interface
questions.learningObjective: supply a lambda that supplies the single abstract method of an interface

options.text: x -> x * x  a lambda body may be a single expression whose value becomes the result.
x -> { x * x; }  a block body may end with an expression statement instead of a return.
options.misconception: believes a block lambda may end with a bare expression statement

options.text: x * x  the parameter list may be left out when the interface has a single method.
options.misconception: believes a lambda may omit its parameter list

options.text: apply(x -> x * x)  the method being implemented has to be named inside the expression.
options.misconception: believes a lambda must name the method it implements

questions.explanation: The rule is that a lambda for a one-method interface is written as the parameters, an arrow, and a body, and a body that is a single expression is taken as the return value, so x -> x * x supplies apply and prints 9. Ending a block with a bare expression statement is tempting because it looks like the same work written out, but a block body that produces no value is not compatible with an int-returning method, and the arrow form needs no method name because the interface's single method is the only possible target.
questions.hint: The interface's only method is the target, so it never has to be named.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: An interface with two abstract methods
questions.learningObjective: predict that a lambda cannot target an interface with two abstract methods

options.text: The compiler rejects it: Calc is not a functional interface, multiple non-overriding abstract methods found.
It compiles and prints 5, because a lambda only has to match the first abstract method it finds.
options.misconception: believes a lambda implements the first abstract method in the interface

options.text: It compiles and prints 5, because add and twice share a name and so are one method.
options.misconception: believes two methods with the same name count as one abstract method

options.text: It compiles and prints 4, because the lambda is bound to twice, which is declared last.
options.misconception: believes the last abstract method declared is the one a lambda supplies

questions.explanation: The rule is that a lambda can only implement an interface with exactly one abstract method, and Calc has two that do not override each other, so javac reports that Calc is not a functional interface and offers no choice to make. Binding the first or the last method is tempting because the two declarations look like variants of one idea and the lambda does have an int parameter, but there is nothing in the syntax to say which method it is meant to be, and an expression body supplies a single body, which is why the interface has to name just one thing to be implemented.
questions.hint: Count the abstract methods before writing anything in lambda form.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A lambda passed to a narrow parameter
questions.learningObjective: trace a call that supplies its one-method interface as a lambda

options.text: 5: the parameter type names the single method, and the lambda body supplies it for 4.
8: a lambda named twice is understood to double whatever it is given.
options.misconception: believes the method's name is applied as the operation on the argument

options.text: 4: the lambda's parameter shadows the argument, so the printed value is the parameter itself.
options.misconception: believes the lambda's own parameter is what reaches the print

options.text: It throws AbstractMethodError, because no class implements the interface in this program.
options.misconception: believes a functional interface needs a named implementing class

questions.explanation: The rule is that the parameter's declared type says which single method has to be supplied, so d.twice(4) calls the lambda's body with 4 and prints 4 + 1 = 5. Reading the method name as the operation is tempting because twice sounds like multiplication, but a name like that is only a label and the body decides, which is exactly the flexibility that makes a one-method interface a good parameter type. No implementing class is needed, because the lambda is itself the implementation for that one call.
questions.hint: The interface names the operation; the lambda body performs it.

questions.topic: A default method using the value a lambda supplies
questions.learningObjective: trace a default method that builds its result from a lambda's contribution

options.text: "hi Ana": the default builds the greeting around the value the lambda supplies for name().
"hi null", because a lambda cannot supply the abstract method a default relies on.
options.misconception: believes a lambda leaves the interface's abstract method unimplemented

options.text: "Ana", because the lambda's body replaces the inherited default method's own body.
options.misconception: believes the lambda body replaces the default method

options.text: It throws AbstractMethodError, because greet() is inherited rather than declared by the class.
options.misconception: believes an inherited default is never properly implemented

questions.explanation: The rule is that a lambda supplies every abstract method of the target interface, so name() returns Ana while the inherited default greet() wraps it, giving hi Ana. Believing the lambda leaves name() unimplemented is tempting because the arrow body was aimed at the single abstract method and the default is not written anywhere, but the default already has a body and needs nothing from the caller, and the two work together, which is what lets an interface own the shared wording while each call site owns only the name.
questions.hint: The lambda and the default each supply one piece of the result.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Claims about narrow interfaces
questions.learningObjective: judge which statements describe the effect of typing a reference narrowly
questions.stem: One interface Sizer declares int size() and another, Growable, extends it and adds void grow(int). A review lists four claims about typing references narrowly. Which claims are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A reference typed as Sizer can be used wherever the code only calls size().
A reference typed as Sizer can be used to call grow(int) on the object it holds.
options.misconception: believes a narrow reference can still call the wider interface's methods

options.text: A parameter typed as an interface declaring only read(int) accepts a wider store instance.
A parameter typed as the widest interface is the narrowest useful type for a read-only client.
options.misconception: believes the widest interface is the narrowest parameter type

options.text: A class that implements an interface exposes all of its methods to every reference to it.
options.misconception: believes implementing an interface exposes every method to every reference

questions.explanation: The rule is that a reference is usable wherever the operations it names cover what the code does, so a Sizer-typed reference serves read-only code and a Reader-typed parameter accepts anything that declares read, which is what makes a narrow type a promise about behaviour rather than about a class. Believing the narrow reference can still reach grow is tempting because the object behind it does have that method, but the reference does not declare it, and choosing the widest interface as the narrowest type inverts the whole point, since it would oblige every future store to offer operations the client never calls.
questions.hint: For each claim, ask whether the declared type covers the call being made.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Adding an operation to a published interface
questions.learningObjective: choose a default body so existing implementers keep compiling after a change
questions.stem: An interface Paid is already implemented by a class Free that was written and compiled last week. A new operation is being added to the interface, and the team wants the existing class to keep working. Which declaration achieves that?

options.text: default boolean paid() { return true; }  the existing class inherits the new behaviour and still compiles.
boolean paid();  the new operation is abstract, so every existing implementer must add it.
options.misconception: believes an abstract declaration is the only way to extend an interface

options.text: static boolean paid() { return true; }  implementers can call it without inheriting anything new.
options.misconception: believes a static interface method is inherited by the implementing classes

options.text: Leave the interface alone and document the new operation, so no implementer has to change.
options.misconception: believes documenting a new operation replaces declaring it

questions.explanation: The rule is that a default body gives the new operation an implementation every existing implementer inherits, so Free keeps compiling and the new behaviour is available immediately, which is the whole reason defaults exist. Declaring it abstract is tempting because that is the shape of a plain interface method, but it converts an addition into a breaking change that every implementer must answer, and a static method is worse still because it belongs to the interface rather than to the objects, so instances of Free would not have it at all.
questions.hint: Ask which form of declaration adds a behaviour without adding a requirement.

questions.topic: A client that only knows the narrow type
questions.learningObjective: trace a helper that compares two implementations through the interface alone

options.text: "test:8": best compares through the Ranked reference and 8 is the larger of the two ranks.
"write:3", because the ternary hands back the first argument whenever its test holds.
options.misconception: believes a condition that holds always selects the first operand

options.text: It throws ClassCastException, because two Task objects cannot be compared with each other.
options.misconception: believes comparing two implementations of one interface needs a cast

options.text: "test:8" only if both tasks are held in an array rather than as Ranked references.
options.misconception: believes narrow references cannot be used to compare two objects

questions.explanation: The rule is that a helper needs only the one operation it uses, so best asks each argument for rank() through the Ranked reference, finds 3 and 8, and returns the task with the larger value, whose toString gives test:8. Expecting the first argument because its test held is tempting when a >= is written, but a condition that holds selects the first operand only when that operand is the intended one, and here 8 >= 3 is true so the second task is returned, which is what makes the higher rank win. No cast is involved because Ranked is the only type the helper knows about.
questions.hint: Work out the value of 8 >= 3 and which operand that selects.
